entities.name: Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu i
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu i, also known as Ankh-af-na-Khonsu, was a priest of the ancient Egyptian god Montu, who served in Thebes during the late Third Intermediate Period, specifically spanning the 25th (Kushite) and early 26th (Saite) Dynasties, a period roughly from 747 to 664 BCE. His primary historical significance stems not from his contemporary political or military actions, but from the posthumous rediscovery of his funerary stele, known as the Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu or the Stele of Revealing, which became a foundational artifact for the early 20th-century occult movement of Thelema. He was the son of Bes-en-Mut I, a priest of Montu, and Ta-neshet, indicating a lineage within the Theban priestly elite.

His role as a priest of Montu, the falcon-headed war god of Thebes, placed him within the powerful religious administration centered around the Karnak Temple Complex. While details of his life are scarce, his elaborate funerary stele (inventory number EA 963 at the British Museum) provides crucial insights into the religious beliefs and iconography of the period. This painted wooden stele, dating to approximately 680 BCE, depicts Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu making an offering to the seated god Re-Horakhty, with the goddess Nut arched above, symbolizing the heavens. The hieroglyphic text on the stele includes an invocation to Nut and a declaration of the deceased's spiritual journey, reflecting standard Egyptian funerary practices aimed at securing eternal life.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu i's funerary stele, rediscovered in 1904, became the central sacred text for Aleister Crowley's Thelema movement, profoundly shaping 20th-century Western esotericism and influencing millions of practitioners.
